item.title: Local learning with imperfect analog synapses
item.description: arXiv:2610.27910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog in-memory computing delivers efficient neural network inference at the edge, but systems deployed in non-stationary environments may need to adapt in situ to locally acquired data. Backpropagation faces two structural obstacles here. Its global error transport lets stochastic write errors compound across layers, and its backward pass demands bidirectional, high-precision peripheral circuitry absent from inference-oriented crossbar arrays. We introduce Channel-wise Spatial Gradient learning (CwSG), a strictly local, forward-only rule that trains each convolutional layer by rewarding spatial variation in its feature maps. In simulations replaying the measured trajectories of 1,189 phase-change memory and 1,268 filamentary memristor devices, CwSG learns with single, unverified, sub-1 V pulses. It matches backpropagation on phase-change memory with 59-fold fewer pulses and outperforms it by 53 percentage points on highly variable filamentary memristors, with 8-bit forward converters and without transposed crossbar reads or network-wide activation storage. Analog training thus becomes a problem of credit assignment, in which algorithmic design rather than hardware compensation alone overcomes severe programming noise.
item.dc:creator: Th\'eo Dupuis, Adrien Renaudineau, Guillaume Bourgeois, Joel Minguet Lopez, Gabriele Navarro, Jean-Michel Portal, Elisa Vianello, Jacques-Olivier Klein, Damien Querlioz

item.title: Sustainable Processing-in-DRAM Integration and Replacement for Transformer Inference Servers
item.description: arXiv:2610.27345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Processing-in-DRAM (PID) accelerators are emerging as a sustainable alternative to GPUs for transformer model inference. They bring compute to data, mitigate the memory bandwidth limitation, and reduce the overall energy footprint. Yet, carbon analysis of PID accelerators is covered for only a limited set of hardware and workloads. In this work, we present a carbon modeling framework for PID-enabled inference servers that captures embodied carbon along with idle and active operational carbon. Our evaluation spans three GPU baselines, six PID architectures, and eight transformer workloads. Additionally, we propose an aging-aware model that finds the carbon-optimal replacement period for PID accelerators over a 10-year horizon. Across evaluated configurations, our analysis shows that including PIDs in AI inference servers increases the total embodied carbon by at most 2.5\%, while the total carbon is reduced by up to 1.14$\times$ for encoder and 1.04$\times$ for decoder transformer workloads. The results also depend on GPU selection for pairing, where introducing PID modules in high-end HGX-H100 servers incurs 5.4--5.9$\times$ higher total carbon compared to A100 and H100 servers, due to their larger idle and embodied carbon. Introducing PID modules in higher-end GPU servers, compared to the A100-only baseline, increases (decreases) the total carbon-delay product (CDP) for encoder workloads (decoder workloads).
item.dc:creator: Bipin Thapa Magar, Ishan Thakkar

item.title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2610.27362v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification. This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration. For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm's requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead. Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification. We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction--solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems. The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators. The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking.
item.dc:creator: David E. Bernal Neira

item.title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.27371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide for latency--accuracy trade-offs.
item.dc:creator: Bipin Thapa Magar, Ishan Thakkar, Sudeep Pasricha

item.title: Green Light: Carbon-Aware Design of Photonic Transformer Accelerators at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2610.27376v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Migrating transformer inference to the edge requires sustainability considerations that encompass both operation and manufacturing, rather than operational energy alone. Silicon photonics enables high-bandwidth, low-energy matrix multiplication; however, existing microring-resonator-based Dot Product Unit (DPU) organizations have been tailored to convolutional computations and evaluated using analog signaling without accounting for embodied carbon footprints. We adapt three DPU organizations (AMW, MAW, and MWA) to transformer inference workloads and extend each organization to stochastic signaling, yielding six organizations in total. We then calculate their embodied and operational carbon per inference. Across five transformer models and four foundry grids, the photonic system achieves improvements of four, four, and six orders of magnitude in Energy-Delay, Carbon-Delay, and Carbon-Energy Product, respectively, relative to CPUs, while also being compared against H100 SXM5 GPU and TPU v5p baseline systems. Analog-to-stochastic conversion increases die area by 4.3-4.6x and embodied carbon by 4.4-4.8x, while reducing operational energy by approximately 91% and causing embodied carbon to equal or exceed operational carbon per inference. Importantly, the DPU organization and signaling scheme, rather than the foundry grid, are the key determinants of carbon impact. Consequently, the fastest organization (MWA) is not necessarily the most carbon-efficient, whereas MAW-Stochastic offers a favorable balance between sustainability and performance.
item.dc:creator: Bharat Bhatta, Ishan Thakkar

item.title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
item.description: arXiv:2610.28342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, Jose Garcia-Alonso, Juan Manuel Murillo, Antonio Brogi

item.title: BERS: Locally Optimal Continuous Algorithm for Maritime Weather Routing with Just-in-Time Arrival
item.description: arXiv:2605.31533v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Maritime weather routing must optimize route geometry under dynamic wind-wave conditions, obstacle constraints, and fixed-arrival requirements. We present B\'ezier Evolve and Refine Strategy (BERS), a two-stage framework that combines global evolutionary search (CMA-ES) with local variational refinement (FMS). Routes are parametrized as B\'ezier curves and evaluated with dense along-path sampling, enabling smooth trajectories while preserving practical feasibility constraints and accounting for mid-segment effects. We evaluate BERS on synthetic benchmarks designed to stress seven operational criteria: continuity, obstacle avoidance, dynamic adaptation, flexible objective design, constant-load feasibility, just-in-time arrival, and local optimality. Across these tests, BERS matches or improves published baselines while maintaining robust convergence under challenging flow fields and land geometries. We then validate the method on real ocean data using hourly ERA5 forcing over 366 daily departures in 2024 for two trans-oceanic corridors (Atlantic and Pacific), with a physics-based model of an 88m cargo vessel with optional rigid wingsails. In real-ocean experiments, route optimization alone reduces mean propulsive energy by 23--59\% versus great-circle baselines of the same propulsion mode. Combined with wind-assisted propulsion, total savings reach up to 75\%. These results show that BERS provides a practical and scalable foundation for just-in-time, energy-efficient weather routing in maritime decarbonization workflows.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Precioso, Francisco Su\'arez, Javier Jim\'enez de la Jara, Rafael Ballester-Ripoll, David G\'omez-Ullate
